newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE chief sees EMU as biggest challenge ahead.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE chief sees EMU as biggest challenge ahead.

text.p: The advent of a single European currency will present derivatives giant LIFFE with its biggest challenge in the years ahead, its chief executive said.

The euro currency under European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is due to start in 1999. The London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) sees EMU not only as a chance to build up its market share but also as a concern.
"Clearly EMU is the thing we have to be most concerned about," LIFFE chief executive Daniel Hodson told Reuters in an interview. "And that concern is on many levels."

The challenge is not only in terms of producing popular products but also in areas such as the exchange's technical systems and its ability to handle the billions of euros worth of trading that is set to take place.

"The other great risk is that in hopefully achieving a significant victory in EMU terms that we ignore the rest of the exchange. We are working very hard to make sure that we don't get completely subsumed in the EMU struggle," Hodson said.

Under EMU, participating countries will have one currency, the euro, and therefore one set of short-term interest rates. At the long end of the curve, the only difference in yields will be down to credit perceptions rather than currency risk.

As a result, contracts such as Euromarks and possibly Eurolire are set to be merged into one euro short-term interest rate future, while the need for more than one long-dated bond future is questionable.
But Hodson is optimistic about LIFFE's future, not least because some of its contracts could stick around even after the 1999 launch date.
Indeed, the one factor which is most often cited as a drawback for London as a financial centre -- Britain's hesitation about joining EMU -- is for LIFFE a potential plus.

"We're in a particularly favourable situation in London because it's very unlikely that sterling will be in in the first round and therefore our sterling products, which are quite a significant number, will be excluded (from EMU)," he said.
"It looks increasingly less likely that Italy will be in and therefore Italian products will be excluded."
Some also argue that once European credit markets merge under EMU they will become a bigger force to be reckoned with. Under this scenario, derivatives trading could become even more popular.
LIFFE is for the moment focusing on grabbing the most of this potentially bigger pie. Hodson said LIFFE's success in this area was demonstrated by the volumes of its post-1999 interest rate futures.

Both LIFFE and French rival the Matif list interest rate contracts with maturities after the EMU launch date. But Hodson noted much higher open interest in LIFFE's Euromarks maturing after 1999 than Matif's Pibor contracts.
Hodson extols the attractions of open outcry trading and sees this as one of the chief reasons why LIFFE will be able to fend off rivals such as Frankfurt's DTB, which uses electronic trading.
